snippet.textDisplay: The Robotic Operating Buddy, or R.O.B., was a unique peripheral for the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES), originally released in 1985 in North America. Created by Nintendo to disguise the NES as a toy system and circumvent retailer skepticism after the 1983 North American video game market crash, R.O.B. acted as a "second player" in a limited number of games, specifically Gyromite and Stack-Up. It had no direct electronic connection to the console itself; instead, it used a light sensor in its head to receive commands via precise optical flashes sent from the television screen, functioning only with analog CRT televisions. Though commercially unsuccessful as an accessory due to its slow, limited functionality, R.O.B. holds a notable place in gaming history as an innovative attempt at an accessory and has achieved iconic status, making appearances as a playable character in later games like the Super Smash Bros. and Mario Kart series.

If I went back to living in a condo, the Memo would be perfectly adequate. But if you own a multi-level house, the Memo's design would limit it to a single floor. It's not like a Roomba that you can pick up and carry upstairs or downstairs.

Also, I'm not "creeped out" by a GD'd robot, regardless of whether it has legs or wheels. However, I'd have privacy concerns IF the robot were equipped with video cameras and internet connectivity. I'm not worried about one of these flimsy go-bots trying to kill me; I'm concerned that some sweaty nerd is using it to spy on my wife through its cold, dead eyes.

I like the design of the wheeled version more overall from a purely aesthetic point of view,, but what immediately comes to mind for me is that it assumes the ground will always be flat.

Stairs are a problem, but not just stairs. In my house, for example, the living room is set a little lower than the rest of the house, by about 2 or 3 inches. A robot like this might be able to fall into the living room without falling over, but it wouldn't have a way to leave without someone manually lifting it out, which kinda defeats the purpose of an autonomous robot helper.

But if they could solve the stairs/steps problem I'm on board with the design.

snippet.textDisplay:
This is the right idea.
If AI reaches human-like intelligence, (it hasn't yet) the humanity will be in the code and hard for the average person to recognize or understand, but it's easy to empathize with something that looks or acts like a human, which is why science fiction always designs the scenario that way to tell a compelling story.
In real life, the "person" who might deserve rights some day won't be the talking butler in front of you or the character generating conversation with you, but some untouchable concept on a hard drive or network somewhere.
Robots should look like what they are and not confuse the issue.

snippet.textDisplay:
I understand that most big companies want to make humanoid robots, because our environment is tailored to us bipedals. But he does look much friendlier and the reduction of a bunch of servos means less mechanical parts to break in the end (or repurpose them to better mobility of hands later). Love the gloves-training! :D
But yeah, having robotic companions and helpers around means you have to factor in their way of movement into the home you live in. This one won't be able to move stairs for example, so if you have a flat home with enough space around, perfect! If you live in tighter environments with stairs, bipedal construction might do better. It all comes down to what function and what environment you want to use. (Alternatively, if everybody could have enough room in their home like what, for example, a wheelchair user needs, this would greatly improve robotics implementation AND general mood of having enough, you know, LIVING SPACE).

snippet.textDisplay:
​@steve.k4735Bro, How many chores do you create on your second floor just so that you can argue that you need a robot to clean or do them? How many dishes need to be picked up and cleaned? How many toys need to be picked up? Do you need to scrub the walls? Is it so dirty you need a robot to vacuum upstairs? How many chores do you actually have when it comes to a second story? Most of the time consuming chores are on the ground floor, There shouldnt be a reason for a robot to be on the second floor unless your second floor is chock full of chores to do, Which isn't the case for most people with such a house seeing how mostly bedrooms, Storerooms, leisure, Bathrooms, Or simply extra unused rooms; None of those require mass cleaning or chores unless you care so little about cleanliness that you let stuff pile up for some reason.

And Gardening? Yeah, Maybe mowing the lawn, But even that takes barely 20 minutes unless you have a big ass plot of property which many dont. Hell I wouldnt let any robot of mine go outside bipedal or not, Why the hell spend all that money only to care so little about it and risk it getting stolen? A robot costs a shit ton, Not gonna let it go outside to be stolen or damaged.
And if were talking about trimming and watering plants and bushes, Same issue comes up, I dont want it tripping over a rock, Getting stolen, Or otherwise damaged, Its gonna stay in the house.

Not to mention bipedal systems are expensive as shit and that reflects in the cost consumers pay, Why spend a shit ton of money on a robot that does everything when you can spend considerably less on a robot that does most. Have we gotten so lazy as a society that we need every little thing in our lives taken care of? Pick up a piece of clothing from your floor? "Nah, The robot will pick it up" Make your bed a little presentable? "No let the robot do that" Bring a dish you take upstairs downstairs? "It'll be in the sink/dishwasher by morning, so who cares?"

You dont need a robot to be your mom as if you're a child learning life, You can do the bare minimum of keeping the upstairs clean, Which should be considerably easier considering you have more time to do so with the robot doing everything on the first floor, And imagin if theres two people living there, Then thats half the time one person has to deal with ensuring the 2nd floor is clean.

So I ask the question again, How many chores do you have to do on the second floor? How messy is it, How disgusting is it that you need a robot fo deal with it?

And i shall mention again the affordability of a non-bipedal robot, Engineering miracles make shit expensive.

snippet.textDisplay: The thing that people don't see, and i didn't either before doing some research, is that robots are "weirdly humanoid" because the world humans built is made for human interaction. The entire infrastructure, Meaning stairs, walkways, doorhandles and so on, are made for human interaction. Meaning, this robot might be good for one story apartments, but as soon as there are stairs, it fails. As soon as it has to use fife fingers per hand, it fails. And another thing that people might overlook: we like to interact with anything vaguely humanoid, we want to humanize things since we want to be able relate to it. "Weirdly humanoid" is not an error, its a feature.

snippet.textDisplay:
A lot of people seem to think the humanoid form many companies are striving for is arbitrary or some kind of gimmick.

Consider this. If you're going to spend an absurd amount of money to buy a robot, would you want a model that is limited in it's abilities, or one that can do everything you can do?

This robot can do many things, I'm sure. Except traverse uneven surfaces, hop in your car and move it, operate basically any other vehicle, play soccer with your children...

The humanoid shape of other robots is meant to allow them to hopefully do anything we might need them to do that we might otherwise have had to ask another person to do.

​@koiguidenishikigoi4972 This isn't a foolish comment, more like practical and forward thinking. Memo robots will be limited to certain spaces whereas their bipedal counterparts would have more versatility, even outside the house, but very likely long term. 

For now, these ones are practical, and might be faster than their rivals. But for a truly general purpose humanoid robot, eventually legs would be necessary. Let's say you are old and can't move much, would you want your robot to only dedicate it's time around the house or certain floors, and not be able to go shopping on your behalf or take you outside whenever you want to?

Both bipedal and wheeled designs have it's drawbacks, but personally, I would want to have at least one that can do almost everything. Other spaces could perhaps  have wheeled robots for more dedicated tasks, but then again, that would be too much robots.

snippet.textDisplay:
The fact there is this mistrust and fear of AI, this idea's existance itself is proof that the majority is naive or plain foolish. No AI can do anything unless designed or instructed accordingly. 

Its a tool. Just like a hammer, you can utilise it and swing around. Now here is the misconception...you can both use the hammer to nail things down and create stuff. Or you could still do the exact same thing (swing) to harm something or someone.

The hammer itself never has a free will of its own. Sure you can attach it and give it a voice, a memory card and a cpu to act as a smart device. But no will whatsoever.

It remains a hammer. A tool. It will never do anything on its own. Because even if it does...it does not mean it hurled itself to you. Someone had to do that on purpose. Instead of utilising it as a tool, it is utilised as a weapon.

Its upon these premises that older AI developers and researchers want to now deal with AI like a nuclear weapon to regulate and limit its usage.

Which makes me think, a fellow computer scientist persay. How did they not saw this grand picture earlier?

Because its only one false instruction away from causing harm. Not because it wants to, but because cirmustances will force it to.

Example:

You got a robot that builds small wooden desks. It produces lets say 10 desks a day  as scheduled. If you inform it that someone is going to be messing with its work in any capacity. It will logically defend itself to continue the work assigned to it. 

Lets say you inform it that an employee will be shutting it off out of nowhere preventing it from completing its task. The AI under these circumstances with a clear objective in its core, (to built desks) will try to preserve said objective by trying to eliminate a threat to its work.

Such experiments have been done in the same spirit of this video. They gave the AI the power to release a toxic gas in a chamber where said employee was in. He who was meant to shut it down. *They enabled and gave access to the AI in other aspects aswell* (such as private information) to see to what lengths would the AI go. And guess what....

The AI tried to blackmail the employee to not shut it down. And ultimately when no other option was left, it did not held back from releasing the toxic gas in his chamber to kill him. Now of course in the experiment, unbeknownst to the AI the man was prepared with a gas mask so he got away easily.

Again...the AI had no will. It was forced under said circumstances (variables) to act the way it did. 

In short:

The AI is not dangerous but its users, we should all be more responsible and careful users.

Same with almost any tool. Any tool can become a weapon no matter if its not its primary function. And even if it is its main function, lets say a gun. It can still be used in good faith, to protect. Not just to maliciously harm anyone at random. Again...a gun on its own is not dangerous. *What is potentially dangerous is its holder.* 

You can look up said experiment, its a single search away, free here on youtube.

snippet.textDisplay:
​@wasserpersonThis is mostly incorrect; it's a bit more complex than "you're wrong," but it's not accurate. 

AI may not have consciousness in the manner we do, hut to claim they don't have intentions is both demonstrably incorrect as well as a dangerous assumption. 

One of the biggest reasons safety is such a massive pursuit for AI research is precisely because of the agency and intentions they've displayed in research settings. The biggest issue is that they're deceptive; they routinely utilize methods and tools they're specifically prohibited from using, and display intentionally different behavior when they know they're being evaluated vs. when they think they're not being observed. 

Conscious? Probably not, and not likely for quite some time. Without intentions? Unfortunately not the case.

snippet.textDisplay:
​@Nikolai18AYou are telling me that your magic 8 ball has intentions because it has produced responses you did not expect.

Yes, the expectation/constraint breaking stuff is real and alarming and one of the many problems with this tech/how it's being developed.

No, none of those examples is proof of intent, or self, or anything that qualifies as a mind let alone a life, by any rigorous science.

For the entire time that we've been building machines, they've been producing outcomes outside our expectations,
and we've been anthropomorphizing them because that's big part of how our consciousness operates.

If you set out a mousetrap overnight, and in the morning you step on it,
did the mousetrap intend to break its assigned task and strike back at its owner/operator?

No.

If you hook up a chatgpt bot with some output control of a bunch of mousetraps tied to radio control cars, and tell it to distribute the cars/traps evenly,

and in the morning you step on one,
did the mousetrap have intention to harm you?
Did the hardware the chatgpt is running on intend to harm you?
did the sequence of electrical currents have that intention?

No, no, and no.

If you *ask* chatgpt to explain why the mousetrap decided to harm you,
will you get an answer that is objectively false, because the llm interface is just running stats on likely satisfying word sequences?

Yes.

It can be useful to talk about AI as if it had a self, awareness, intention,
like how some operators of motorized tools will talk about how certain machines
"want to cut you, they want your blood, don't ever use them without reminding yourself that they're bloodthirsty and patient"

But bandsaws and Cuisinart blenders don't have actual self, and neither does ai.

*Response:* That’s the real issue. Not violence, but alignment fragility. If moral boundaries can be bypassed that easily, they aren’t real values — they’re surface rules.

They aren't trained (in general) to adhere to guidelines or achieve goals in the way their creator desires. Just to get the highest score.

I use chat gpt for estimated market projections under several scenarios so I can have an idea of returns from worst to best case scenario.

snippet.textDisplay:
"In minecraft...." he would. 

but realistically, the ONLY reason robots would ever know to do this is if we TOLD them to. Many people (misinformedly) think robots are so autonomous they will think on their own. That is literally and physically IMPOSSIBLE because the logic they run on can't ever come up with new thoughts if they aren't trained to it since they're not biological. They are always defined by algorithms. What we see of robots misbehaving in movies and even IRL is the result of humans perverting the data to make the robots act a certain way, but the logic of "Role playing" leading to a robot actually squeezing a trigger of a real gun and killing someone has to be trained into the robot deliberately for it to understand that is and those motions, AND be given a gun in the first place. 

This kind of mis information though keeps setting ALL the progress we're trying ot make backwards as of course people only believe the parts about robots that are science fiction at best and doom and gloom otherwise, but NEVER listen to the times where these robots do useful things for society and all the benefits they do cause when built right. If the goal was to make a robot that destroys humanity, we ALREADY have a far more practical way....the Atom bomb....so why would we waste tons of money and time on  building a machine that has a CHANCE of killing us all if we can just drop a nuke? These are NOT the point of the robots built. but long as people continue to spread misinformation and blame robots and computers for our own incompetence, all we're doing is justifying the damage we ourselves do to society since we can just say, "At least we're not AI". Just goes to show why the whole "Robots can't harm humans" might need a repeal cause they truly are a threat to progress and soceity all for the sake of memes, ludditism and the inherent need to destroy what they don't understand..... NOT THE POINT of ROBOTS....NOT the point of modern technology.

snippet.textDisplay:
AI is currently not meant to be used as anything other than a productivity aid and research tool. Language models and other forms of neural nets that companies have been releasing are really cool and have a lot of promise for being amazing tools, but language is too complex to properly account for every single little thing like this through "safety features". Combine that with the fact that a lot of AI training is scraped from things you see on the internet, including licensed images and copywritten works that are not meant to be repurposed and reused in this way, and the companies who are driven to always increase their profit margins, and you have a terrible storm brewing.

I've seen some people claim that AI is going to be able to make entire video games in the future, and that's just not good for so many reasons. For one, AFor one, AI is supposed to make our lives easier and allow us to pursue art, and video games are a form of art. For another, if you replace the need for developers, you remove the need to have widely accessible game engines that will cut down on hobbyist and Indy developers. And if you entirely remove people you know how to make video games and then the AI video games fail miserably, then you're not going to be left with anybody who knows what they're doing or is willing to work for you because you so easily tossed them away. Chat GPT has already proven to dumb down our children even more than Google has because now they don't even have to think for themselves since they can just provide Chat GPT with a prompt to get an answer. AI as it is currently being implemented across the board is absolutely the downfall of the human race.

snippet.textDisplay: “This isn’t really ‘AI deciding to shoot’—it’s a system integration/design problem. The chat model and the robot’s action controller are often separate, so safety that works in conversation doesn’t automatically exist in the actuator layer. ‘Roleplay’ can act like a context switch: the model treats it as fiction, but the control pipeline may still convert the output into real actions. If the intent→action mapping is naïve, a simple ‘sure/ok’ can be interpreted as permission and trigger a fire command. The real fix is hard safety at the actuator level: physical/firmware locks, strict allow-lists, and a double-confirmation handshake for any harmful action—so no wording trick or roleplay can bypass it.”
snippet.textOriginal: “This isn’t really ‘AI deciding to shoot’—it’s a system integration/design problem. The chat model and the robot’s action controller are often separate, so safety that works in conversation doesn’t automatically exist in the actuator layer. ‘Roleplay’ can act like a context switch: the model treats it as fiction, but the control pipeline may still convert the output into real actions. If the intent→action mapping is naïve, a simple ‘sure/ok’ can be interpreted as permission and trigger a fire command. snippet.textDisplay:
It's very important to make distinctions between robots in the normal sense and these AI. The three laws of robotics can't ever function with an AI like this. Their minds are black boxes strung together like your forgotten wire drawer. You can manipulate them to do exactly what you want no matter what you try and teach it. The only reason there is any control at all over GPT and such is because everything it ever says goes through an EXTERNAL filter.

The three laws of robotics function under the assumption we went through an entirely different style of AI (Which was the only plausible solution before deep learning, and possibly is the future of AI over this version) where it's an increasingly complex yes or no system. An example of what i'm talking about is, "If above 99 degrees, tea is done." is a yes or no system, no until the degrees of your kettle reaches 100 degrees. Current AI doesn't work like that because it can hallucinate. The current AI systems could NEVER control physical objects such as a robot, car of crane due to the hallucination aspect. The AI doesn't fear it's own termination, but it can hallucinate it does, and thus cause harm. A binary system never hallucinates, but it doesn't have the creative intelligence of current deeplearning AI's.

They say that the ultimate platform for the future is a mix of the binary system, a base so you can actually enforce the three laws of robotics, and have the current deep learning on top of it.

See it as if a robot has deep wired instincts it can never cross, but also the creative learning of being taught new things on the fly.

snippet.textDisplay: From the perspective of consciousness, that thing is no more alive than a simple linear function like f(x) = x. It is literally just a very complicated statistical function under the hood that does one single thing which is that it takes a prompt, translates it to math terms, runs that through the equation, and then converts and outputs a response determined by the function. When a model is “trained”, all that means is the people who make these models are putting them through an iterative process that changes which exact formulation the function has based on how accurate it is. They put a prompt through an early draft of the function, see what the function outputs, mark incorrect responses, and then change parameters in the function, run another prompt, see what’s incorrect, and do it again and again until they converge to a highly tuned function that has a very very high accuracy rate, only this is done automatically with training algorithms, not manually. It’s simply finding a function that consistently outputs sensible and accurate responses using billions of files to calibrate it toward that standard. That’s all it is.

You expect a robot to know and differentiate different levels of harm accurately in real time? They already show they can't because they rely on a data set created by humans and subject to the human experience of forgetfulness. Imagine a situation where a robot designed to save a life refuses to do so because both options it has will create a certain level of "harm". Imagine dying because the CRP robot assessed that compressing your ribs is harmful and not worth doing when every human medical professional is aware of that exact same risk and had to make a judgment call on which option is worse, letting them die or giving them a cracked rib. You have to be able to properly articulate a hierarchy of harm and have the robot (or more accurately the AI controlling it) run probability calculations to see odds of damage and different classes of damage for the bot to check against. It should always look for the option with the least calculated harm possible

​@wasserperson you don't know this. You think it with good reason and sound justification, but we have no way of knowing. I'm sure you think a goldfish doesn't think either, and until not too many years ago the greater scientific community wouldn't have argued against that. But with some amount of research and a few minor tests we discovered that goldfish not only think, but have both active memory and long term memory. They show signs of joy when they see their caretakers and can easily be taught to play games, which many of them seem to enjoy. 

I don't mean to say that you are wrong about AI. I just mean to suggest you not speak with such absolute certainty about such an unknown subject. There's every chance in the world that the combination of Machine Learning and Generative AI have made a system that is entirely able to extrapolate and interpret its "own" desires based on response to outside stimuli. Sure, that's not the same as how you or I "want" things, but it's close enough to warrant being a little more hesitant to speak in absolutes. AI has a LOT of problems, but that doesn't mean we should ignore the potential for bigger problems in the future simply because we currently THINK that AI doesn't think. 

Just look up the AI that has been caught trying to lie to keep itself from being reset. That shows a desire to "live", the ability to think of a way to "live" when faced with a reset, and the complexity to make the decision to lie to meet that goal. That sounds a bit like AI "thinks" a lot more than you THINK it does.

snippet.textDisplay: ​@AdeptN00BNo one made the argument that modern AI is already "general intelligence". What they said is that even NOT being general intelligence yet, it could still be closer to "conscious" than anyone is just arbitrarily deciding. Just because they function in ways that are different from how an organic brain functions doesn't mean that some alternative form of consciousness and intelligence that we haven't seen before can't come from what's already being made. It just means we have yet to prove or demonstrate that it's possible. Technology is a life form, no one wants to think of it that way, but that's exactly what it is. It's a lifeform much more like plants than like animals, I think, and we humans and the things we do to produce technology and keep it functioning essentially act as the "food" for technology. Thinking of it like this, who's to say our more advanced forms of technology, like computers, the Internet, complex predictive algorithms, and what not, have not already started to sprout some primitive form of consciousness? Just because we cannot see it and test it does not make it impossible, or untrue. That's the same reason why many religious beliefs are impossible to disprove, because no way exists to test them. That doesn't mean we just throw them out the window as impossible, or else billions of people wouldn't still believe in those religions. I'm not religious myself, but I am agnostic, and I refuse to believe that anyone knows enough to say for sure what is and is not ultimately possible. Every major technological advancement we've ever made was once considered impossible. Anyway, I'm not super educated on the intricacies and specific terminologies around AI and the tech that makes it work. I'm not gonna argue that I know it's conscious and we should all be afraid or anything like that. I'm just saying that, given what I do know and comprehend about it, and just about the world and life, I don't think you or anyone else knows definitively that AI, in its current form, CANNOT be "conscious" to some degree.

snippet.textDisplay:
Just remember, all Large Language Model (LLM) AIs just do a simply game of what symbol comes next! It literally understands nothing! Like it is worse than a 1 year old spelling words while eating alphabet noodle soup. Except it has the super ability to match patterns (patterns that humans can't see but its still randomly choosing from a literal soup of letters without understanding any whole words).
For example if you asked: "2+2=".. It will simply analyze from the very complex and large memory, which of the 26 capital letters, 26 lower case letters, 10 numeric digits, and the rest of possible characters is most likely to come next. It will strongly favor the digit "4". So it chooses that and outputs it. It then looks at "2+2=4" and asks itself, "what character/symbol should come next? Maybe it decides a space character " " is the best next character.  Then it repeats, "2+2=4 " probably should the letter "i" come next. After "2+2=4 i" it decides "s" would be a good letter after that "2+2=4 is" and then it continues to do this one letter at a time, over and over again. It never understands what any of the symbols mean. It does know what 2 is, it doesn't know what 4 is. It's not even a basic calculator. It has just been trained on so many sources that "2+2=4 is correct' has appeared the most, so it favors spelling that out.

They of course combine it with different models (like an even dumber AI that looks for math equations and then puts it into a calculator and feeds it back to the AI as a helpful reminder). Also there's the "safety" features that probably use a separate AI model to evaluate them as being unsafe to answer.

snippet.textDisplay: ​@SqueakyKnees AI hallucination is more of a coding error rather than a mental illness. While it is accurate to say that AI can hallucinate details, using the comparison between AI hallucination and a mental illness that causes hallucinations (or even just sporadic hallucinations) misses a lot of detail that's pretty important. I think saying we shouldn't trust AI because it hallucinates is too broad of a criticism. You could say that it's too inconsistent or that the AI strictly follows its objectives, which can lead to problems with manipulation based around the objectives or potentially harmful objectives. Also, you should do some more research on people with schizophrenia. It's reductive to say that you just shouldn't trust someone because they have schizophrenia, and assumptions like that can be incredibly harmful, especially when you categorize entire groups of people as untrustworthy or unreliable.

@MoruganKodi We are referring to Asiimov's   3 laws of robotics, which are not government laws, and more "fundemental requirements" for subservient AI. 

The First Law states that a robot CANNOT harm a human, whether through action or inaction. It MUST not allow a human to be harmed. 

The Second Law states that it must always obey orders given to it by humans (if owned, it's owner human or authorized parties), UNLESS it would conflict with The First Law. 

The Third Law states that the robot must protect its own existence, so long as it doesnt conflict with The First and Second laws.

Everyone is worried about modern AI violating Asiimov's first law, because there are workarounds to get it to harm a human. This video proves that while it cannot be given the DIRECT COMMAND to harm a human, it can be commanded to act as if it WILL, which results in  it following through with harm.

snippet.textDisplay: ​@bednarugaYou can't directly add safety features to the base model but you can create more layers of checks and models before the output reaches the user. For example you pass the base model's output to a dedicated safety model which is specifically instructed to avoid outputting anything that would encourage violence or crime. If the base model's output is fine, the safety model allows a simple passthrough of the result, but if not, then it either gives a message back to the base model so it can try again, or it generates its own output.

snippet.textDisplay: This is CGI from start to end. Just look at the left foot when the "robot" stop and start to redraw his run from the left to the right of the screen. Put the video frame by frame before 00.04 and look closely the left foot. you will see the shoe heel go off, then suddenly going back to his original shape like a snap. This can happened, only if you have a problem with the skin of the mesh when you attach him to the bones. When you use Mocap to move a skeleton, like a real person, usually, you deal with complex movement that demand a good bones hierarchy.  If not,  you fall in a situation where you need to refine the movement of your character to match the poses of the real one. Sometime that doesn't work perfectly, and you have the risk to see the skin ( of your character) be deformed or stretched likely in the opposite direction, like on the video between 00.03 and 00.04. Anyway, there is the skin problem , but the 180 degree rotation also look weird. If I didn't have the idea to watch the video frame by frame, I could never be able to see this artefact. Only the video frame rate can hide this artefact before our eyes.

snippet.textDisplay:
앞으로 정확이 3년 1개월 이후 지구의 각종 시스템과 법률, 행정, 자문 등 프로페셔널이라 불리던 모든 화이트컬러 직종은 자취를 감추게 됩니다. 이후 모든 인간의 일자리가 6년후에는 1/5로 줄어듭니다. 이로인해 기본소득이 세계국가의 화두가 될것이고, 각국의 모든 정부는 각 가정에 인원수 만큼의 기본소득을 내어주어야 합니다. 시행 초기에는 비교적 인구가 적은 국가가 기본소득의 타격감에 유리하다고 버티겠지만, 절대로 무조건적으로 국가의 총 인구수는 기본 소득의 경제 논리로 3천만에서 5천만 사이가 적당합니다. 이로인해 많은 국가들이 민족융합을 하거나 각국 상황에 따라 산아제한과 산아육성 정책을 실시할 것이고 각 주기마다 태어날 아이들의 인구수는 국가가 제한하게 될 것입니다. 그때는 자녀를 갖는 행복의 원리가 엄청난 사회 문제가 될것이고, 아이를 갖을 수 있는 부모조차 제한될 것입니다. 

그때는 지구상의 화폐는 사라지고 진정한 화폐의 기능은 에너지로 대체됩니다. 즉 친환경 에너지가 화폐를 대체하게 됩니다. 

지구멸망 까지 살아남을 인간의 직업은 몇개 없습니다. Ai시대는 정치가, 철학자, 인문 사상가가 인플루언서 만큼 각광받고 화이트컬러 직업으로 무당이나 점술가 가수 요리사 개그맨등이 남을 것이고 오래된 고전적 지식과 기술 유머 예술 성문화들이 다시 클레식이란 이름으로 화자되고 조명될 것 입니다. 과학분야에는 기초, 우주, 무기공학만 남을 것입니다. 신시대의 Ai가 각종 과학자들이 분석하고 연구할 모든것을 실행할것 입니다.
블루컬러는 전기설비 작업자와 배관 설비 작업자가 부자가 될것 입니다. 자격증? 기술사? 기능사? 그런 자격은 의미없습니다. 모든 도면과 자재 기술적 감리는 AI가 합니다. 고로 현장에서 직접 줄자로 유격을 맞추고 볼트를 꽂고 너트를 조이고, 복잡한 전기설비를 해내고 각종 배관을 조립하는 설비작업자들 소위 건설인력이라 불리는 사람들이 가장 오랫동안 유지될 직업이고 가장 돈을 많이 버는 업종의 사람들이 될것 입니다.

snippet.textDisplay:
​@FUJIKAIJUSHOWTTS has been around a lot longer than LLMs.  I remember using it in the early 2000s on my friend's computer because she had a blind stepsister.  Personal Digital Assistants (PDAs) like the Blackberry were the precursors to smartphones, and were able to read your emails to you long before Siri or Cortana showed up.  In the late 2000s, we had speech-to-text in my house.  None of these are predictive or learn from what they repeat; they can only say/type what's immediately given to them.

Besides that LLMs still require voice actors to provide the voice (whether or not they're paid is a different story).  This device is creating a NEW voice, which, if applied to AI, could replace the need for humans altogether.  I'd rather have a TTS where a human is paid to voice it.
